design_detail: Systematic review with four-level random-effects meta-analyses and multiple meta-regressions (R, metafor; effect estimates nested in trials and studies) of placebo-controlled experimental trials that gave a single dose of THC and measured simulated or on-road driving, or a driving-related cognitive skill, within 12 hours. 80 studies, 155 trials, 3454 participants, 1534 outcomes, of which 1011 were eligible for quantitative synthesis. Peak-effect meta-analyses by performance domain (within 1.5 h of inhaled or intravenous THC, 1.5 to 3.5 h after oral THC); meta-regressions of inhaled THC (all, regular and other cannabis use) and oral THC to model how impairment varies with dose and time, and to predict a recovery time.
can_establish: The average size of THC-related impairment on laboratory driving and cognitive measures shortly after a single dose, and, in people who use cannabis less than weekly, how that impairment tends to grow with dose and fade with time in laboratory studies, as modelled across trials.
cannot_establish: A safe time to drive for any person (no crash outcome, averaged effect sizes, a recovery threshold chosen by the authors); how long impairment lasts in people who use cannabis weekly or more (their model explained nothing); impairment beyond the few studies that tested after about 4 to 6 hours (later predictions are extrapolations of a fixed recovery rate); effects of real-world products, repeated use or alcohol combined; effects in women (71% of participants were men).

sample.recruitment: Web of Science and Scopus, 2000 to April 2020, English-language articles only, with a secondary search using modified terms; reference lists of two earlier reviews hand-searched (pp. 176-177).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Placebo-controlled trials (within- or between-subject) giving a single acute dose of THC and testing driving or a driving-related skill within 12 h; excluded THC combined with another active treatment, more than one dose before testing, unreported dose or timing, duplicate reports and inadequate reporting; studies scoring below 50% on the Rosendal quality scale and studies of clinical populations were excluded from the quantitative synthesis (pp. 176-179).
sample.demographics: 71% men overall (Table 3, p. 180); mostly healthy adults; cannabis use grouped as regular (weekly or more in all participants) or other (mostly occasional) (Table 2, p. 178).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; 31% of outcomes from healthy-participant studies were ineligible for quantitative synthesis (p. 188).
sample.selection_effects: Two databases, English only, from 2000, no grey literature or trial registries; authors of 2010-2020 studies were contacted for data; values were digitized from graphs where needed. Regular-use trials were few and clustered at 20-60 min after one narrow band of doses (exposure field) (p. 186).

exposure.measurement: THC dose given in each trial, in absolute milligrams (body weight was rarely reported, so doses could not be made relative) (p. 187).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: single doses; in the eligible trials mean doses were 20 mg oral, 14 mg vaporised, 32 mg smoked and 2.5 mg intravenous (Table 4, p. 180); in the meta-regressions doses ranged 3.7-94 mg inhaled (interquartile range 10-26 mg) and 2.5-50 mg oral (10-25 mg), and post-dose test times 1-480 min inhaled (45-240 min) and 60-720 min oral (120-360 min) (p. 182). Predictions in Table 9 are for a reference dose of 20 mg, and Figs. 2 and 3 also show 10 mg (pp. 186-187). In the other-use inhaled model doses were 3.7-69 mg (interquartile range 10-25) at 1-480 min (60-240); in the regular-use model 90% of outcomes were at 20-60 min and 71% at 21-26 mg (pp. 182, 186).
exposure.polysubstance: Trials combining THC with another active treatment were excluded; placebo treatments (such as placebo alcohol), tobacco and other cannabinoids were allowed (p. 176).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Regular-use studies standardized prior use differently: at least 24 h abstinence, overnight abstinence, usual use, or not stated (p. 186).

comparison.matching: Within-subject designs predominated; effect sizes standardized against the SD of the change, with the correlation imputed (R = 0.53) where not reported, or against the pooled SD for between-subject designs (p. 178).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level; tolerance, recent use and body weight varied and were partly captured only by the regular-or-other grouping.

outcomes.instruments: Driving simulator or on-road measures (lateral control including standard deviation of lane position, speed and its variability, car-following headway, reaction time) and cognitive tests grouped into domains: divided attention, tracking, information processing, conflict control, fluid intelligence, reaction time, fine and gross motor function, sensory discrimination, time perception, sustained attention, working memory (Table 1, p. 177).
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study quality scored with the Rosendal scale (mean 62%, SD 10, range 43-93%) (p. 179); individual scores in a supplement not read.
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment = negative Hedges' g against placebo; recovery = the predicted time at which g reaches -0.25, described as the level at which effects are unlikely to have a meaningful impact on performance (Table 9 footnote, p. 186); no external validation of this threshold is given.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 17 peak meta-analyses were run (Table 7) plus four meta-regression models.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; screening by two investigators independently (p. 176); data extraction procedures are described against a Cochrane checklist without saying whether extraction was duplicated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Peak effects, Hedges' g (95% CI) (Table 7, p. 184): divided attention -0.28 (-0.36 to -0.20); tracking -0.42 (-0.58 to -0.25); information processing -0.38 (-0.55 to -0.21); conflict control -0.34 (-0.42 to -0.25); fluid intelligence -0.37 (-0.46 to -0.27); reaction time -0.28 (-0.43 to -0.13); fine motor -0.36 (-0.60 to -0.12); sustained attention -0.23 (-0.37 to -0.10); working memory -0.36 (-0.52 to -0.20); sensory discrimination +0.09 and time perception -0.05, not significant. Driving: lateral control -0.24 (-0.41 to -0.08); lane weaving (SDLP) -0.29 (-0.47 to -0.11); driving reaction time -0.47 (-0.70 to -0.23); speed +0.14 (-0.01 to +0.29), speed variability -0.16, headway -0.03 and headway variability -0.24, not significant. Meta-regression (Table 8, p. 185): in the combined inhaled model regular use +0.17 (+0.06 to +0.28, p = 0.003) and vaporising -0.09 (-0.17 to -0.01) against smoking, but pseudo-R-squared 0.0; regular-use model, no covariate significant; other-use inhaled model, dose -0.0082 per mg (-0.0112 to -0.0053) and time +0.0005 per min (+0.0004 to +0.0007), pseudo-R-squared 0.64; oral model, dose -0.0087 per mg, curvilinear time term significant, pseudo-R-squared 0.28.
analysis.covariates: Performance domain, cannabis use (regular or other), route (smoked or vaporised), dose, post-dose time (plus a quadratic term for oral THC).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol registration is mentioned; methods are said to be reported according to PRISMA-P 2015 (p. 176).
analysis.selective_reporting: Robustness to the imputed correlation (R = 0.2 and 0.8) is reported only in Supplementary File 5, not read; no publication-bias assessment; predicted recovery times in Table 9 are given without intervals.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors note few studies of regular cannabis use and of longer post-dose intervals (4-6 h) (p. 188).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Shortly after THC, most driving-related measures were impaired by small to moderate amounts (g about -0.23 to -0.47), while speed was not (drivers tended to go slightly slower). In people who use cannabis less than weekly, impairment grew with dose and faded with time; at the reference dose (exposure field) the model's aggregate effect reached the authors' threshold at 300 min smoked, 350 min vaporised and 480 min oral, with domain predictions from under 60 min to 530 min after inhaling (lane weaving 427-472 min, information processing 486-530 min) and 415-665 min after oral THC. Regular use was associated with less impairment, but its duration could not be modelled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says most skills would recover within about 5 h and almost all within about 7 h of inhaling the reference dose, and that individuals should wait at least 5 h after inhaled cannabis before safety-sensitive tasks (p. 175; repeated p. 188). Gaps: (1) Table 9 shows lane weaving and information processing beyond 7 h at that dose, and only 4 of 8 domains within 5 h when smoked (editors' count); (2) the waiting advice turns a dose-specific average into a rule for all inhaled use, while the Discussion itself says there is no universal answer and that dose matters (p. 184); (3) the recovery threshold is not linked to crash risk; (4) predictions past about 4 h rest on few data and assume steady recovery, as the Limitations concede (p. 188).

timeline.event: Hartman et al., simulator study of cannabis and lane weaving with and without alcohol, among the trials in this field.
This review: first meta-analytic estimate of the duration of THC impairment of driving-related skills, by the authors' account.

replication.where_it_stands: The main quantitative synthesis of how long acute THC impairment lasts in laboratory studies. Its duration estimates are model predictions with no intervals, fitted mostly to tests within 4 hours, and apply to people who use cannabis occasionally.

funding.funder: No specific grant; three authors receive salary support from the Lambert Initiative for Cannabinoid Therapeutics, a philanthropically funded centre for medicinal cannabis research at the University of Sydney (p. 188).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Sydney (Lambert Initiative, Brain and Mind Centre) and Griffith University; the review includes trials by its own authors' group (for example Arkell et al., 2019).

what_would_settle_it: Controlled studies that test driving repeatedly from 1 to 12 hours after realistic doses and products, in people who use cannabis daily as well as occasionally and in women, reporting individual recovery curves and crash-relevant outcomes rather than averaged standardized effects.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, single-dose THC, placebo comparison, driving and driving-related outcomes, and the 12-hour window are specified.
No registration or published protocol; PRISMA-P is cited only as a reporting standard.
Placebo-controlled experimental trials only, as required to isolate the acute drug effect.
Two databases from 2000, English only without justification, no grey literature or registries; reference lists of two reviews hand-searched.
Two investigators screened independently, with a third for discrepancies.
Extraction against a Cochrane checklist, but duplicate extraction or checking is not described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The main text gives only a shortened flow diagram; excluded tasks and outcomes with reasons and the full PRISMA flow are in Supplementary Files 1 and 2, not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Doses, routes, timing and use frequency summarized by domain (Tables 3 to 6); per-study details only in Supplementary File 4, not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The Rosendal scale (combining Jadad, PEDro and the Delphi list) covers randomization, blinding and reporting, but collapses them into a percentage; scores per study only in a supplement.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Multilevel random-effects models handle dependent effect estimates; the imputed correlation was varied in sensitivity analyses. Caveats: peak analyses pool across doses, routes and use frequency, and recovery predictions extrapolate a linear fade.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Studies under 50% on the quality scale were dropped, but no analysis examined how quality affected the estimates.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion and conclusions do not consider the quality of the primary trials.
I-squared, Q and variance components reported; meta-regression used to explain heterogeneity; residual variance and its possible sources discussed (p. 187).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and salary support declared; no conflicts.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 could only be judged from supplements that were not read. AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence because several critical items are not met (no registration, a restricted search, no account of primary-study quality in the interpretation, no publication-bias assessment), whatever item 7 turns out to be. The statistical modelling is sophisticated and transparent, and the peak impairment estimates rest on many placebo-controlled trials; the weakness lies in the duration predictions, which have no intervals, depend on a chosen threshold and extend beyond most of the data. The review can be cited for the size of acute impairment and for the direction of dose, time, route and use-frequency effects; its recovery times can be cited only as model predictions for occasional use, not as safe waiting times.

key_findings.finding: Included: 155 trials from 80 studies, 3454 participants (71% men), 1534 outcomes, of which 1011 from 108 trials (2583 participants) were eligible for quantitative synthesis. Mean Rosendal quality score 62% (SD 10, range 43-93%); six studies scored under 50% and were excluded from quantitative synthesis.

Peak effects (Hedges' g, 95% CI): divided attention -0.28 (-0.36 to -0.20), tracking -0.42 (-0.58 to -0.25), information processing -0.38 (-0.55 to -0.21), conflict control -0.34 (-0.42 to -0.25), fluid intelligence -0.37 (-0.46 to -0.27), reaction time -0.28 (-0.43 to -0.13), fine motor -0.36 (-0.60 to -0.12), sustained attention -0.23 (-0.37 to -0.10), working memory -0.36 (-0.52 to -0.20); sensory discrimination +0.09 (-0.08 to +0.25) and time perception -0.05 (-0.30 to +0.20) not significant.
key_findings.note: Minus signs checked on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Peak effects on driving: lateral control -0.24 (-0.41 to -0.08), lane weaving (SDLP) -0.29 (-0.47 to -0.11), driving reaction time -0.47 (-0.70 to -0.23); speed +0.14 (-0.01 to +0.29), speed variability -0.16 (-0.35 to +0.02), car-following headway -0.03 and its variability -0.24, not significant. The authors read the speed trend as drivers widening their safety margins.
key_findings.locator: Table 7, Car Driving rows (p. 184); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 186, left column)

key_findings.finding: Inhaled THC, combined model (579 estimates): regular cannabis use (weekly or more) associated with less impairment (+0.17, +0.06 to +0.28, p = 0.003) and vaporising with more than smoking (-0.09, -0.17 to -0.01, p = 0.021), but the model left most heterogeneity unexplained (pseudo-R-squared 0.0). Regular-use model (59 estimates): no covariate related to effect size, so duration could not be predicted for regular use; 90% of these outcomes were measured 20-60 min after dosing, within one narrow band of doses (exposure field).
key_findings.locator: Results 3.3.1, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 182); Table 8, upper two panels (p. 185); Discussion (p. 186, right column)

key_findings.finding: Inhaled THC, other (mostly occasional) use, 481 estimates: impairment increased with dose (-0.0082 in g per mg, -0.0112 to -0.0053) and decreased with time (+0.0005 per min, +0.0004 to +0.0007), and differed by domain (information processing, lane weaving, tracking and divided attention most sensitive); pseudo-R-squared 0.64. Dose and time ranges are in the exposure field.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.3.1, 4th paragraph (p. 182, right column); Table 8, third panel (p. 185)

key_findings.finding: Oral THC (243 estimates, all from other use): impairment increased with dose (-0.0087 per mg) with a U-shaped time course (delayed peak, predicted at 283 min, then recovery); pseudo-R-squared 0.28, so the authors advise more caution.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.3.2 (p. 182); Table 8, lowest panel (p. 185); Table 9 footnote d (p. 186); Discussion (p. 187)

key_findings.finding: Predicted recovery time (to g = -0.25) at the reference dose (exposure field) in other use, smoked / vaporised / oral, in minutes: aggregate 300 / 350 / 480; divided attention 383 / 428 / not calculable; tracking 386 / 430 / 573; information processing 486 / 530 / 557; conflict control under 60 / 71 / 665; reaction time 232 / 276 / 492; fine motor - / - / 415; sustained attention under 60 / under 60 / -; working memory 277 / 321 / -; lane weaving (SDLP) 427 / 472 / -. Predicted peak effects at that dose: aggregate -0.40 smoked, -0.42 vaporised, -0.32 oral.
key_findings.note: No intervals are given for any prediction; the footnote for the Aggregate row (f) is missing from the table.

key_findings.finding: The Discussion summarizes that most driving-related skills recover within about 3 and 5 h of inhaling the lower and the higher reference dose respectively, almost all within about 5 and 7 h, and that oral impairment of most skills takes about 8 h to subside after the higher reference dose (doses in the exposure field); the conclusion says individuals should wait at least 5 h after inhaled cannabis before safety-sensitive tasks, depending on dose, while also stating there is no universal answer to how long to wait.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 184, right column); Discussion (p. 187, left column, top and right column); final paragraph (p. 188)

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: English only; 31% of healthy-participant outcomes ineligible for synthesis; models assume a fixed rate of recovery; trials contributing many estimates weigh more; studies testing after 12 h excluded; few studies of regular use and of longer intervals (4-6 h); women underrepresented and doses absolute rather than per body weight.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraphs on residual variance (p. 187) and on further limitations (p. 188, left column)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Discussion say almost all skills recover within about 7 h of inhaling the reference dose, but Table 9 predicts 427 min (smoked) and 472 min (vaporised) for lane weaving and 486 and 530 min for information processing at that dose; and only 4 of the 8 inhaled domains with values (smoked) fall within 5 h, so the 5-hour figure matches the aggregate row rather than most skills (editors' count).
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline durations are more favourable than the review's own table; the table's values should be cited, as predictions.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 9 has an Aggregate Effect row marked with footnote f, but no footnote f is printed; the aggregate is described only in the text as an average across domains graphed in a supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: How the aggregate recovery time was computed cannot be checked from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The combined inhaled model is reported with significant covariates and also with a pseudo-R-squared of 0.0, that is, no improvement over a model without moderators.
reporting_issues.consequence: The regular-against-other difference comes from a model that explains almost none of the variance; it is consistent in direction with the separate models but its size is uncertain.
